new_statements.quote: Storch (1997) says that "Wãpha has more consonants than most related Jukun languages and has four distinctive tones." Without a thorough analysis of the other Jukun languages, we cannot confirm this claim. [...] In our data, tone is only marked on a few vowels, so we cannot make any confident statements about tone.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Wãpha is reported (second-hand, from Storch 1997) to be a tone language with four distinctive tones; the only accessible first-hand description (Decker et al. 2021) neither confirms the tone system nor mentions stress or accent at all. No source states where word stress falls.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not mentioned in any source examined.
new_statements.exceptions: None; Decker et al. explicitly decline to make claims about tone.
new_statements.domain_note: Wordlist citation forms only (348-item SIL Nigeria list, singular nouns and infinitives), elicited in Kumbur, Mavo and Dampar villages; no connected speech, no phrase-level prosody discussed.
new_statements.identity_note: Wãpha = Jukun Wase = Meek's 'Wase Tofa'; Decker et al. 2021 cover the Kumbur/Wase Tofa variety and the Mavo and Dampar varieties (Mavo possibly a separate language). Do not confuse with Kona Jukun = Jiba [juo] (subject of the Adelberger & Storch 2008 text that the earlier scan mis-tagged as a Wãpha phonology) or with Wukari Jukun = Wapan [juk] (subject of Meek's 1931 tone remark).

sources.locator: Sec. 6.3 Phonetic inventory, p. 12 (Storch quotation) and p. 14 (tone remark); PDF pp. 18 and 20 of 47
sources.source_kind: database or survey citing another work
sources.note: Sec. 6.3 'Phonetic inventory' (pp. 12-14) gives tentative consonant and vowel tables from 348-item wordlists; quotes Storch (1997) that 'Wãpha has more consonants than most related Jukun languages and has four distinctive tones' and adds 'In our data, tone is only marked on a few vowels, so we cannot make any confident statements about tone' (p. 14). No mention of stress or accent anywhere; wordlists (App. E) carry no tone or stress marks.

sources.citation: Glottolog 5.3 languoid page waph1238 and reference pages 585855, 158405, 674933; rogerblench.info Jukunoid folder (Wayback CDX); Endangered Languages Project page 5036
sources.note: Glottolog lists no grammar/sketch/phonology for Wãpha (n_desc_refs = 0). Blench's Jukunoid folder holds only Jibu and Kuteb items, no Wãpha. ELP page has no bibliography.
Phoneme tables copied from Decker et al. 2021 (cites SIL entry 88593); nothing on tone or stress.

sources.citation: Meek, C. K. 1931. A Sudanese Kingdom: an ethnographical study of the Jukun-speaking peoples of Nigeria. London: Kegan Paul. xxxiii+548 pp.
sources.note: Pp. 1-2 list six Jukun 'dialects' incl. Wase Tofa (= Wãpha) with a 20-word comparative table and remarks on pronominal affixes; p. 14 says 'In the Wukari dialect tones are significant' with examples (Wukari = Wapan, not Wãpha); appendix 'Wase Tofa Dialect' wordlist (~95 items) has no tone or stress marks. Nothing on stress for any dialect.
